beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string only from an environment variable (e.g. DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit it to source control, logs, or README files; load secrets from a secret store (Azure Key Vault) in production.
Reuse a single long-lived MongoClient/connection pool instance for the lifetime of the Node.js process (create once on startup and share it); do not open/close a new connection per HTTP request.

Configure the MongoDB driver connection options to use TLS, an appropriate max pool size (maxPoolSize), sensible serverSelectionTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS, and enable retryable writes if available (retryWrites=true) to improve reliability under transient network errors.

Design your partition key for high cardinality and even distribution (e.g. customerId or contentId) so traffic and storage distribute across partitions; include the partition key in queries to avoid costly cross-partition scans.
For collections with time-limited interaction events (sessions, ephemeral history), create a TTL index on the timestamp field so old documents are automatically deleted instead of growing unbounded.

Keep documents reasonably small; store large binary blobs or full text in a dedicated content store (or compress them) and keep the DocumentDB documents to the metadata, embeddings, and pointers required for retrieval to reduce RU consumption and latency.

Store vector embeddings as a typed array/array of float32 (or numeric array) and normalize them (unit length) if you will use cosine similarity so comparisons are stable and efficient; avoid storing embeddings as strings.

Create appropriate indexes for your frequent filter and sort patterns (e.g. compound indexes on {customerId, lastInteractionAt} or on content metadata fields) so metadata filtering can be executed server-side before any vector kNN step.

For vector search, prefer server-side kNN/vector index usage (cosmosSearch/vector index) when available instead of fetching many candidates and running nearest-neighbour calculations client-side; server-side ANN scales and reduces data transfer/RUs.

If you must run client-side kNN (as a fallback), pre-filter by metadata using indexed queries to reduce candidate set size, then compute cosine or dot-product similarity on the application host and only return top-K results.

When creating a server-side vector index, specify and document the index type and ANN algorithm parameters (e.g. HNSW: M, efConstruction; DiskANN/IVF: index type, numLists) explicitly so index behavior and resource usage are deterministic.

Avoid cross-partition vector queries when possible; either co-locate vectors that will be queried together under the same partition key or perform a controlled multi-partition query pattern (pre-filter then kNN per-partition) because cross-partition kNN can be expensive or unsupported.

Project only necessary fields in queries (use projection) when returning documents (e.g. omit embeddings when fetching metadata) to reduce RU costs and network transfer; fetch embeddings only when needed for similarity computation.
Use exponential backoff with jitter for retries on transient failures, limit total retry attempts, and make write operations idempotent where possible to avoid duplicate side effects.

Configure and monitor RU/s (or autoscale RU) to match expected query patterns (vector queries and heavy filtering increase RU consumption); validate RU usage during load and prefer autoscale or burst-capable tiers for variable traffic.

Instrument queries with explain() and server-side profiling tools (or the MCP/documentdb diagnostics) to verify indexes are used, to inspect query plans for vector $search usage, and to optimize filters before relying on client-side workarounds.

Protect personally identifiable information (PII) and avoid logging customer profiles or embeddings; redact or hash identifiers in logs and ensure access control so only authorized services/users can read sensitive collections.

For agent memory and conversational history, store summaries and relevant vector embeddings instead of full transcripts to limit storage, speed similarity searches, and stay within document size limits; use TTL for short-lived memory.

Limit the number of candidates pulled from DB for client-side similarity (e.g. 500–5000 depending on embedding dimension and latency budget) and tune batch sizes; compute top-K via an efficient in-process ANN library if local vector workloads grow.

When index creation fails via the driver, use the managed cluster/console or the MCP/documentdb admin tools to create and inspect vector indexes and verify that the server-side vector index feature and the chosen API version/wire protocol are supported for that cluster.

Use small, focused collections for different data types (profiles, interactions, content_pieces, agent_memory) with indexes tailored to each collection's access patterns rather than a single catch-all collection.
Apply rate limiting and circuit breaker patterns around expensive vector-search endpoints to protect the database from traffic spikes and to give predictable latency for the service.

Store embedding dimensionality as metadata with each collection (e.g. embedding_dim) and validate incoming embeddings match expected dimension at ingest time to avoid silent corruption of vector indexes or incorrect similarity scores.

Avoid synchronous blocking long-running vector computations inside HTTP request handlers; delegate expensive candidate scoring to background workers or use async batch jobs and return streaming or cached results to clients.

Document any required MongoDB wire protocol version and feature flags (e.g. MongoDB 7.0 compatibility, vector index capability) in the repo README and .env.example so operators know what cluster features are required and can validate the cluster before running the sample.
